stem: The effect of an introduction of a carbon tax of $23 per tonne of CO2 emissions on the market for electricity that is generated from burning coal would be to

options.A: shift the supply curve to the left and cause a contraction in supply
options.B: shift the supply curve to the left and cause a contraction in demand
options.C: shift the demand curve to the left and cause a contraction in supply
options.D: shift the demand curve to the left and cause a contraction in demand

trap_note: A tax on producers raises their costs, so the SUPPLY curve shifts left. Price rises and consumers respond by moving along their demand curve - a contraction in DEMAND. The 21% who said contraction in supply put a shift and a movement on the same curve, which cannot happen at once.

stem: In a given year, an increase in the trade-weighted index (TWI) is least likely to

trap_note: A higher TWI makes exports dearer and imports cheaper, so net external demand (X-M) gets WORSE. The 18% who chose the income distribution option picked something a rising dollar genuinely does cause - importers gain, exporters lose - which is why it reads well.

stem: Suppose Australia’s interest rates are increased while the interest rates of its major trading partners remain unchanged. Which one of the following combinations is most likely to result?

trap_note: Higher Australian rates make holding the dollar more attractive, so fewer people sell it. Supply of AUD DECREASES and the TWI rises. The 21% who had supply increasing described what happens when rates FALL.

stem: Assume average wages in the national economy have increased by 5 per cent per annum and average labour productivity has increased by 2 per cent per annum. Which one of the following is the most likely outcome of these increases?

options.A: an increase in real wages and a rise in the operating profits of Australian businesses
options.B: an improvement in equity in income distribution as a result of the likelihood of declining unemployment
options.C: an increase in inflationary pressures, reducing the price competitiveness of Australian exports and import-competing goods
options.D: a significant increase in business confidence levels, resulting in much higher levels of investment by business owners in new capital resources

trap_note: Wages up 5% against productivity up 2% means unit labour costs rise 3%. That is cost inflation, and it damages price competitiveness. The 19% who chose higher profits had it backwards - costs rising faster than productivity squeezes margins, it does not widen them.

options.D: the purchase of new computers for the neighbourhood library by a local government

examiner_comment: The payment of salaries to public servants is classified as government current (consumption) expenditure given that the benefits provided do not extend beyond the current budget period (e.g. one year). Unemployment benefits is a government transfer payment (neither G1 nor G2); Options C and D relate to Government Investment (G2) spending.
trap_note: Current expenditure is day-to-day operating spending, and salaries are the clearest case. The 33% who chose unemployment benefits picked a transfer payment — and transfers are not counted in AD at all. The government buys nothing; it moves money to a household, which then spends it as consumption.

stem: Which one of the following is least likely to result in a decrease in aggregate supply?

options.A: an increase in interest rates
options.B: a slower rate of productivity growth
options.C: an increase in the number of people retiring
options.D: a decrease in the availability of capital resources

examiner_comment: B is the answer because productivity is still increasing (despite a slower growth rate) which increases aggregate supply. Option A is less valid because higher interest rates can have negative supply side effects via an increase in the costs of production (debt servicing costs). Increases in retirement (Option C) and less available capital resources (Option D) are likely to reduce aggregate supply as the quantity of labour and capital resources falls.
trap_note: VCAA's reasoning: a SLOWER RATE of productivity growth still means productivity is rising, so AS still increases. 56% chose interest rates, and VCAA accepts that higher rates can reduce AS through debt servicing costs. Interest rates work on both sides. In the exam you can use either — lead with AD, it is the bigger impact.

stem: The payment of dividends to Australians holding shares in foreign companies will be recorded in the balance of payments as

options.A: acredit in the capital and financial account
options.B: a debit in the capital and financial account
options.C: a credit in the current account
options.D: a debit in the current account

examiner_comment: Dividends received represent an inflow of funds (credit) that represents the servicing costs (for foreigners) who have sold shares to Australian investors. These flows are recorded in the current account as a credit. (If the receipt of funds was related to the sale of the shares by Australian investors then this would have been recorded in the CAFA.)
trap_note: Dividends received BY Australians from shares held overseas are money flowing IN, so a credit, and income earned on investment sits in the current account. The 34% who chose the capital and financial account picked the account that records buying and selling the shares, not the income they pay.

stem: Cyclical unemployment is least likely to be caused by

options.A: a decrease in the size of the government’s budget structural deficit
options.B: a decrease in the world price of iron ore. C
options.C: lowrates of economic growth in China
options.D: negative interest rates

examiner_comment: Negative interest rates incentivises borrowing and credit based consumption or investment. A lower structural deficit (Option A) is more likely to reduce AD and increase (structural) UE. A decrease in iron ore prices and slower growth in China (Options B and C) will tend to have a negative impact on both national income and AD, increasing pressure on unemployment.
trap_note: Cyclical unemployment comes from weak AD. Negative interest rates encourage borrowing and spending, which lifts AD and REDUCES cyclical unemployment. The 28% who chose the smaller structural deficit picked something that does cut AD — which makes it a cause, the opposite of what the question asked.

stem: ‘A cyclical factor that might cause Australia’s current account balance to worsen is

options.A: ahigh rate of economic growth in China
options.B: ahigh rate of economic growth in Australia
options.C: high energy costs due to the closure of coal-based power plants
options.D: lower productivity growth in Australia than in its major trading partners

examiner_comment: A high rate of growth in Australia typically leads to an increase in import spending relative to export receipts, reducing the BOGS and decreasing the CA balance for reasons related to changes in economic growth (or the business/economic cycle). A high rate of growth in China (Option A) improves the CA balance. The remaining two options (C and D) are examples of structural factors that can worsen the CA balance.
trap_note: Cyclical means tied to the business cycle. Strong growth in Australia pulls in imports faster than exports grow, worsening the current account. The 45% who chose lower productivity growth named a real problem, but a STRUCTURAL one. Check which type the question wants before you read the options.

stem: Australia’s terms of trade is likely to deteriorate if

options.A: the Australian dollar appreciates
options.B: export prices rise faster than import prices
options.C: there is excess supply of iron ore in world markets
options.D: there is an increase in productivity growth in Australia’s major trading partners

trap_note: The terms of trade is export prices over import prices. Excess supply of iron ore drives export prices down, so the ratio falls. The 28% who chose an appreciation picked something that moves export and import prices together — and the causation usually runs the other way, with a high terms of trade lifting the dollar.
